cues.headline: Start with one whole.
cues.text: Meet a sandwich. The entire rectangle is one whole. Before we can name a fraction, we need to know what our whole is. Trace its outside with your finger. Every share will come from this same sandwich.

cues.headline: Two pieces. But is it fair?
cues.text: Watch the sandwich split into two pieces. One piece is much bigger than the other. There are two pieces, but they are not halves. To make halves, both friends must get the same amount.

cues.headline: Equal shares make halves.
cues.text: Now the cut moves to the middle. Both pieces have the same size. One coloured piece is one out of two equal parts: one half. The other piece is a half too, even though it is not coloured.

cues.headline: Two halves rebuild the whole.
cues.text: Watch the second half join the first. Nothing is missing and nothing overlaps. One half plus one half makes one whole. Imagine sharing this sandwich with a friend. Explain why equal size matters more than simply counting two pieces.

questions.prompt: Which sharing makes halves?
questions.explanation: Halves are exactly two equal parts of the same whole.

questions.prompt: One sandwich is shared equally between two friends. How many equal parts make the whole sandwich?
questions.explanation: Two equal halves fit together to make one whole.

cues.headline: Four equal parts in one whole.
cues.text: Here is a fresh whole, cut into four equal parts. Count every part, including the empty ones. There are four altogether. That total gives us the bottom number of our fraction: the denominator.

cues.headline: Choose three of the four.
cues.text: Watch three parts light up, one after another. The top number counts these selected parts. It is called the numerator. We selected three, so the numerator is three. The whole still contains four equal parts.

cues.headline: The numbers tell two different jobs.
cues.text: Read the fraction as three quarters. The three counts selected parts. The four counts all the equal parts in the whole. Follow the labels beside the fraction, then match each number to the strip above it.

cues.headline: Change the selection, keep the pieces.
cues.text: Now only one part is coloured. We have one quarter. The numerator changed from three to one, but the denominator stayed four. We changed how many parts we chose; we did not cut the whole differently.

questions.prompt: In 3/4, what does 4 tell us?
options: Four equal parts in the whole
questions.explanation: The denominator counts all equal parts in one whole.

questions.prompt: Five of eight equal parts are coloured. What is the numerator?
questions.explanation: The numerator counts the selected parts, so the fraction is 5/8 and the numerator is 5.

cues.headline: One equal part has its own name.
cues.text: One selected part makes a unit fraction. The top strip shows one half. The bottom strip shows one sixth. Each fraction has a numerator of one, but the parts have different sizes because the wholes were divided differently.

cues.headline: Same whole. More parts. Smaller shares.
cues.text: Both strips have exactly the same length. Watch how much space the coloured share takes in each. Splitting a whole into six equal parts makes each part smaller than splitting it into two. One half is larger than one sixth.

rows.caption: The whole stays the same size

cues.headline: Six sixths fill the whole.
cues.text: The six equal pieces light up in order. Each piece is one sixth. Count them as they fill the strip. Six copies of one sixth make one whole. The denominator tells us how many of these equal pieces we need.

cues.headline: You control the equal shares.
cues.text: Move the equal-parts slider. The whole stays the same size and one piece stays selected. Try two parts, then eight. Predict which share will be smaller before moving the slider. Explain what changes and what stays the same.

questions.prompt: For equal-sized wholes, which fraction is largest?
questions.explanation: A half is larger: dividing the same whole into fewer equal shares makes each share bigger.

questions.prompt: How many pieces of size 1/6 make one whole?
questions.explanation: Six sixths make one whole: 6 × 1/6 = 1.

cues.headline: One whole journey, from 0 to 1.
cues.text: A fraction is also a number. Here, the distance from zero to one is one whole journey. Our marker starts at zero. A point halfway along this journey will represent half of the whole distance.

cues.headline: Count spaces, not marks.
cues.text: Divide the journey into four equal spaces. Notice the five marks, including zero and one. We count the four spaces between them. Each space is one quarter of the full distance, so each step adds one quarter.

cues.headline: Three equal steps land on 3/4.
cues.text: Follow the marker as it takes three quarter-steps from zero. The first step reaches one quarter, the second reaches two quarters, and the third reaches three quarters. There is still one quarter-step left before one whole.

cues.headline: After halfway. Before one whole.
cues.text: Two quarters is halfway, which is also one half. Our marker is at three quarters, one step beyond halfway. It has not reached one. Point to the space between one half and one: that is where three quarters belongs.

questions.prompt: Where is 3/4?
questions.explanation: Three quarter-steps travel farther than halfway but do not reach one whole.

questions.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 has four equal intervals. How many quarter-steps from 0 reach 1/2?
questions.explanation: Two quarter-steps reach 2/4, which is the same number as 1/2.

cues.headline: Begin with one half.
cues.text: The coloured piece covers one half of this whole. Keep your eyes on its right edge. We are going to cut the pieces smaller without adding any colour or changing the size of the whole.

cues.headline: New cuts. Same coloured amount.
cues.text: The second strip is the same size, but each half has been split into two. The coloured half now contains two quarters. Its right edge lines up exactly with the half above. The names differ, but the amounts match.

cues.headline: Both counts change together.
cues.text: One selected part out of two becomes two selected parts out of four. Both counts have doubled. One half and two quarters are equivalent fractions. Multiplying the top and bottom by the same positive whole number keeps the amount unchanged.

cues.headline: Cut again: four eighths.
cues.text: Now the lower whole has eight equal parts. Four are coloured, and their combined length still matches the half above. One half, two quarters and four eighths all describe the same amount. Trace the matching coloured lengths to check.

questions.prompt: Which fraction equals 1/2?
questions.explanation: Two of four equal parts cover the same amount as one of two equal parts.

questions.prompt: Fill in the missing numerator: 1/2 = ?/8.
questions.explanation: Multiply both numbers in 1/2 by 4 to get 4/8.

cues.headline: Compare pieces of the same size.
cues.text: These two wholes have the same length and each has eight equal parts. Every piece is an eighth of the same-sized whole. That makes the pieces directly comparable. We can decide which fraction is greater by counting selected eighths.

cues.headline: Three eighths on the first strip.
cues.text: Three pieces light up in the top strip. That is three eighths. The five uncoloured parts still belong to the whole, so the denominator is eight. Keep that coloured length in mind as the second selection appears.

cues.headline: Five eighths reaches farther.
cues.text: Now five pieces light up in the bottom strip. Each piece has the same size as a piece above. Five eighths reaches two pieces farther than three eighths. More pieces of the same size give us a greater amount.

cues.headline: Same denominator? Compare the counts.
cues.text: Line up the left ends of both strips with your finger. The lower coloured section is longer. Five eighths is greater than three eighths because five is greater than three. This comparison works because both wholes and both piece sizes match.

questions.prompt: Which of these fractions is greatest?
questions.explanation: With equal wholes and equal denominators, the larger numerator represents more.

questions.prompt: How many more eighth-sized pieces are in 5/8 than in 3/8?
questions.explanation: Five eighths has two more eighth-sized pieces than three eighths: 5 − 3 = 2.

cues.headline: Start with one eighth.
cues.text: Imagine this strip is a melon cut into eight equal pieces. You take one piece. That is one eighth of the melon. The empty positions help us remember that eight equal pieces would make the original whole.

cues.headline: Two more eighths join it.
cues.text: Two more pieces slide into the next positions. Count the original piece and the two new pieces: one, two, three. Altogether, you have three eighths. The new pieces are the same size as the first one.

cues.headline: Add the counts. Keep the piece size.
cues.text: The answer is three eighths. The numerator counts one plus two, so it becomes three. The denominator stays eight because each piece is still an eighth. Adding pieces does not divide the whole into sixteen parts.

cues.headline: Try two eighths plus three eighths.
cues.text: Here is a new combination. Begin with two coloured eighths, then watch three more join them. Count all selected pieces before naming the fraction. The whole still has eight positions. Say your answer aloud, ready for the checkpoint.

questions.prompt: What is 2/8 + 3/8?
questions.explanation: Add the counts: two plus three is five. Each piece is still an eighth.

questions.prompt: Fill in the missing numerator: 1/8 + 3/8 = ?/8.
questions.explanation: Add the counts: 1 + 3 = 4. The pieces are still eighths, so the sum is 4/8.

cues.headline: Begin with five sixths.
cues.text: Five of these six equal pieces are coloured. They represent the cake that remains: five sixths of the original cake. The uncoloured position is still part of our whole, so each piece is a sixth.

cues.headline: Take away three sixths.
cues.text: Three coloured pieces lift away and their positions are crossed out. Count only the coloured pieces that remain: one, two. We started with five sixths and removed three sixths, leaving two sixths.

cues.headline: Two sixths is also one third.
cues.text: The top strip shows the two sixths that remain. The bottom shows one third of an equal-sized whole. Their coloured lengths line up. Two sixths and one third are equivalent names for the same remaining amount.

cues.headline: Your turn: four sixths, take one.
cues.text: Start this time with four sixths. Watch one coloured piece leave. Count the pieces that remain, and keep their size in the name. We still use sixths because the whole still has six equal positions.

questions.prompt: What is 4/6 − 1/6?
questions.explanation: Four sixth-sized pieces minus one sixth-sized piece leaves three sixths.

questions.prompt: Fill in the missing numerator: 5/6 − 2/6 = ?/6.
questions.explanation: Five sixth-sized pieces minus two leaves three sixths.

cues.headline: A whole can be a collection.
cues.text: These eight counters are our whole collection. A fraction can describe part of a group as well as part of a sandwich. Count all eight counters first. We will share this entire collection into equal groups.

cues.headline: Four equal groups of two.
cues.text: The counters are arranged into four equal groups, with two counters in each group. Each group is one quarter of the collection. Eight divided by four is two, so one quarter of eight counters is two counters.

cues.headline: Choose three of the four groups.
cues.text: Watch three groups light up. Each selected group contains two counters. Count them in pairs: two, four, six. Three quarters of eight is six. We chose three groups, not just three individual counters.

cues.headline: Divide into groups, then select.
cues.text: To find three quarters of eight, first divide eight by four to find two counters per group. Then choose three groups: three times two is six. Point to the two unselected counters. They make the remaining quarter.

questions.prompt: To find 3/4 of a collection, what do you do first?
options: Split it into three equal groups
Split it into four equal groups
questions.explanation: The denominator tells us to make four equal groups. Then we choose three of them.

questions.prompt: What is 3/4 of 8 counters?
questions.explanation: Eight split into four equal groups gives two counters per group. Three groups contain six counters.

cues.headline: Plan a picnic with quarters.
cues.text: This picnic sandwich has four equal pieces. You choose one quarter to begin with. Name the whole, count all its equal parts, then count your selection. Those three checks help every fraction story make sense.

cues.headline: Add two more equal shares.
cues.text: Two more quarter-sized pieces join yours. Count the selected parts: one, two, three. One quarter plus two quarters makes three quarters. The denominator stays four because the size of each piece has stayed the same.

cues.headline: Different cuts. The same picnic share.
cues.text: Now cut every quarter in half. The second strip has eight equal parts, and six are coloured. Six eighths covers the same length as three quarters. Changing both counts together gives a different name for the same share.

cues.headline: One idea, in pictures and numbers.
cues.text: Our marker reaches three quarters on the number line. This is the same amount as three of four sandwich pieces or six of eight smaller pieces. Fractions connect equal shares, counts and positions. Use that connection for your final checkpoint.

questions.prompt: A picnic has 16 equal slices. You eat 1/4 of them and a friend eats 3/8 of them. What fraction of all the slices is left?
questions.explanation: One quarter is two eighths. Together you eat five eighths, so eight eighths minus five eighths leaves three eighths.

questions.prompt: A box holds 24 counters. One third are blue and one quarter are red; none are both. How many counters are neither blue nor red?
questions.explanation: One third of 24 is 8 and one quarter is 6. That accounts for 14 counters, leaving 24 − 14 = 10 counters of other colours.
